evergreen_facts.text: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in Frankfurt in 1749; his family home is now the Goethe House museum.
Frankfurt's St. Paul's Church hosted the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament, Germany's first freely elected parliament.
Holy Roman emperors were elected in Frankfurt for centuries and, from 1562, crowned in its cathedral.
Frankfurt lies on the river Main, which gives the city its full name, Frankfurt am Main.
The Römer, a row of medieval buildings on Frankfurt's old town square, has housed the city hall since 1405.
The Eiserner Steg, an iron footbridge across the Main in Frankfurt, first opened in 1869.
The Palmengarten, opened in 1871, is Frankfurt's botanical garden, with glasshouses full of tropical plants.
Apfelwein, a tart apple wine, is Frankfurt's traditional drink, served in taverns in the Sachsenhausen district.
Grüne Soße, a cold sauce made from seven fresh herbs, is a Frankfurt specialty.
The frankfurter, a thin smoked pork sausage, takes its name from the city of Frankfurt.
The Frankfurt Book Fair continues a tradition of book trading in Frankfurt dating back to the 15th century.
Frankfurt's Museumsufer is a string of museums lining both banks of the Main.
The Städel Museum in Frankfurt, founded in 1815, holds European art from the Middle Ages to the present.
Frankfurt's Senckenberg Natural History Museum is known for its large collection of dinosaur skeletons.
Chemist Otto Hahn, who discovered nuclear fission, was born in Frankfurt in 1879.
The forested Taunus hills rise northwest of Frankfurt, topped by the Großer Feldberg.
